title: US Strikes Iranian Rocket Launchers at Larak Island, Ending Month-Long Hormuz Lull as Tanker Hit Near Khasab; Europe's Gas Storage Hits 13-Year Low
subhead: The US military struck Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday — the first direct US attack on Iranian positions in over a month — after Tehran prepared to lay sea mines, and Iran retaliated with missile fire at US bases in Jordan. Brent crude climbed toward $90 as Europe's gas reserves fell to their lowest level since 2013.

sections.heading: Hormuz: US Ends Month-Long Lull With Strike on Larak Island
sections.body:
The US military struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, August 30, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) was observed preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the waterway, a US official confirmed to RFE/RL. US Central Command said it took 'limited, precise action against IRGC mine-laying forces posing an imminent threat,' the first publicly reported direct US attack on Iranian military positions in more than a month. The strike came after a tanker was hit by an 'unknown projectile' while transiting inbound through the strait north of Oman's Khasab, per the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), as reported by Anadolu Agency.

The IRGC vowed retaliation, acknowledging 'the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters,' and later said it fired ballistic missiles at two bases housing US forces in Jordan. Jordan said it intercepted eight incoming missiles that entered its airspace early on August 31, according to RFE/RL. The exchange followed a week in which US Central Command said it had completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.
sections.whyItMatters: The strike signals Washington will use force to prevent Iran from re-establishing its ability to threaten Hormuz shipping, but analysts note the strait is physically open — reduced traffic is driven by the risk of attack, which mine-clearing alone cannot eliminate. Iran can keep harassing vessels with missiles and drones, so the standoff can persist without a return to full-scale combat.

sections.heading: Oil: Brent Climbs Toward $90 as Gulf Attacks Resume
sections.body:
Oil prices rose on Monday, August 31, after fresh fighting erupted in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude gained 1.6% to $89.50 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate rose 1.5% to $84.63, according to CNBC-TV18. Other reports put Brent above $90 as Asian markets and US futures fell. Crude closed out a volatile month, with Brent futures swinging by almost $17 a barrel over the period as a US-Iran peace deal looked unlikely, CNBC-TV18 reported.

The escalation compounds a broader picture: Reuters reported that six months into the US-Iran war, the conflict is hardening into a stalemate that could last well into 2027, with energy markets held hostage and inflation elevated. The war, alongside the Russia-Ukraine conflict, has pushed up petroleum product prices, particularly diesel.
sections.whyItMatters: The renewed tit-for-tat shows the market's 'war premium' is not fading — it is re-pricing on each escalation. With the US-Iran conflict showing no off-ramp, oil remains structurally exposed to Hormuz risk, and the Venezuela deal's promise of lower prices has so far been outweighed by Middle East risk.

sections.heading: Europe: Gas Storage at Lowest Since 2013 as 'Winter Panic' Builds
sections.body:
EU gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level since 2013, feeding a 'winter panic' among traders, The Guardian reported, as cited by Press TV. The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG) put reserves at around 64% as of Friday, versus about 72% on the same date in 2013 and well below the 80% average maintained in recent seasons. The benchmark Dutch TTF front-month contract traded at about €69 per megawatt-hour on Friday, up from roughly €29 at the start of 2026, per EU Today.

Germany, which operates Europe's largest storage system, is at risk of missing its statutory target of 70% full by November 1. Facilities were about 51.5% full on August 25, versus 69% a year earlier, and the storage association INES warned the target would not be met at the current injection pace, EU Today reported. Germany holds around 45 terawatt-hours less gas in storage than a year ago — roughly the Czech Republic's entire capacity. SEB chief commodities analyst Bjarne Schieldrop told The Guardian the crisis will only be resolved when the war ends, 'and no one expects it to happen any time soon.'
sections.whyItMatters: The shortfall stems from weak commercial incentives to inject gas now for winter resale, compounded by Hormuz disruption to Qatari LNG and EU sanctions on Russian supply. Low storage raises the risk of sharp winter price volatility, and Germany's shortfall has knock-on effects across Europe because it holds the largest storage system.

sections.heading: Venezuela: US Moves to Control 65 Billion Barrels, Refill SPR
sections.body:
Washington is moving to take direct control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves through a proposed 100-year concession spanning 17 fields, per a Bloomberg report cited by CNBC-TV18. The US would control 55% of output from a new joint venture and obtain the oil at cost, a US official said. Trump called it 'the biggest oil deal in world history,' and said the crude would be used to replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which held about 289.7 million barrels — roughly 40% of capacity and a 44-year low, after heavy drawdowns under both his administration and Biden's, CNBC-TV18 reported.

Interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez said the project targets production of more than 1.5 million barrels per day across 17 strategic oilfields, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it would bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, per The Epoch Times via NTD. The deal was negotiated by Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Rodríguez, and comes roughly nine months after US forces captured former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal would make the new US-controlled entity the second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, and more than double US oil reserves. But analysts note major infrastructure hurdles remain, and the at-cost oil is unlikely to deliver near-term price relief — the announcement has so far been outweighed by Hormuz risk in the market.

sections.heading: SCO Summit in Bishkek: Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian Meet as Russia Looks East
sections.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian convened in Bishkek on August 31 for the two-day Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit marking its 25th anniversary, RFE/RL reported. Putin has at least nine bilateral meetings scheduled, including with Pezeshkian and Xi, as Moscow seeks to position itself as a counterweight to Western influence. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said 'one of the key subjects' in the Putin-Pezeshkian talks will be the Middle East crisis, and on the agenda is the $25 billion agreement for Russia's Rosatom to build four nuclear power plants in Iran.

Analyst Naser al-Tamimi of MidEast Strategia told RFE/RL the SCO offers Iran broader political cover and expands opportunities for trade in yuan, rubles and other national currencies, modestly reducing Tehran's dependence on the Western financial system — but it is not an economic shield against US sanctions, lacking a fully developed alternative financial architecture.
sections.whyItMatters: The summit is a venue for Russia, China and Iran to coordinate on energy and sanctions circumvention, but its practical limits are clear: it cannot protect members from secondary sanctions. The Rosatom nuclear deal with Iran is a strategic signal of deepening Russia-Iran energy cooperation even as both face Western pressure.

sections.heading: Global South: Bangladesh's Energy Import Bill Doubles as LNG Crunch Bites
sections.body:
Bangladesh's energy import bill reached $10.63 billion in FY25-26, up 107% year-on-year, while stalling nearly Tk35,000 crore in industrial investment across 1,857 pending gas-connection applications, according to a study by the Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI) and Policy Exchange Bangladesh, reported by The Daily Asian Age. National daily gas demand stands at 3,800 mmcfd against effective supply of only 2,420 mmcfd — a 36% shortfall. The crunch traces to a bottleneck in LNG imports, with the Excelerate floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU), capacity 600 mmcfd, shut since a fire on July 21 and only partially restored.

Some of the worst-hit districts face 12-14 hours of power cuts a day, and industrial production capacity around Chattogram airport fell by about 25%. Only two of three targeted LNG cargoes were secured in three tender rounds in August, at rising prices, while domestic gas production has declined for nine consecutive years.
sections.whyItMatters: Bangladesh illustrates how the global energy shock is hitting the Global South hardest — a doubling import bill, chronic load-shedding and stalled investment. The LNG supply crunch, worsened by Hormuz disruption and rising prices, is forcing a poor importer to ration gas between power, fertilizer and industry.

bottomLine: The US-Iran conflict has re-escalated: Washington struck Iranian rocket launchers at Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday — the first direct US attack in over a month — after Tehran prepared to lay sea mines, and Iran retaliated with missile fire at US bases in Jordan. Brent crude climbed toward $90 as the market re-priced Hormuz risk, while Europe's gas reserves fell to their lowest level since 2013, raising the prospect of a volatile winter. The Venezuela deal gives Washington control over 65 billion barrels and a path to refill the depleted SPR, but offers little near-term price relief. At the SCO summit in Bishkek, Russia, China and Iran are coordinating on energy and sanctions circumvention, though the grouping cannot shield members from US secondary sanctions. The bottom line: the war premium is back, Europe faces a storage shortfall, and the Global South is absorbing the worst of the energy shock.
sources: RFE/RL, CNBC-TV18, Anadolu Agency, UKMTO, Reuters, The Guardian, Press TV, EU Today, ENTSOG, The Epoch Times via NTD, Bloomberg (via CNBC-TV18), The Daily Asian Age, MCCI/Policy Exchange Bangladesh, Dhaka Tribune (via Dhaka Online)
